compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Either person may enjoy a last-minute outing or prefer to make plans. What friends notice in one setting does not establish an E/I or T/F preference.

The resemblance comes from the shared S and P. S is sourcing: both more often trust comparable facts and first-hand experience, and neither is much moved by abstract argument. P is outward stance: both more often leave the conclusion until there is enough information, and neither rushes to nail down a schedule or a plan. But those two describe sourcing and stance only, not reaction speed, and not who is more fun — either can plan ahead, and either can act at once when needed.

The difference sits on two axes. E/I is the direction of attention and energy: outward to interaction and the situation, or inward to reflection and one's own experience. T/F is the basis for judgement: whether one standard can be applied consistently, or what this means for the people involved and for what one values. Both axes are used at once; the difference is which is relied on more often.

### One budget, and how to explain "meets spec but not right"

Suppose each is buying a common household appliance, with the same budget, the same use, and the same product pages and reviews. The difference is not who starts looking first, but how each explains "the specs all pass, and it still does not feel right".

One explanation starts more often from checkable conditions: which scenarios this specification covers, whether the missing feature will stick in some use, what the extra money buys, and whether the return policy is clear. The other starts more often from one's own experience and what one cares about: how the last one felt to use, whether this one will get in the way of daily life, and which details one genuinely does not want to compromise on.

Each has a cost. Watching only conditions may bring home something that passes everywhere and is never wanted; going only by fit may mean comparing for a long time and then not buying at all — "I have not met the right one" — or paying more than necessary for one moment of delight. Conversely, either person might focus on value for money when rent is due or compare several models carefully when the choice matters to them. Those are ability and circumstance, not evidence of preference.

What matters is not who is more particular, but which basis is cited first in this trade-off, and where each would give way: accepting a little dislike once the conditions pass, or accepting a little imperfection once it feels right. Both concessions occur in the same person.

### Why Se and Ni are shared while the whole judging set changes

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te. Position by position: Se is dominant for ESTP and second for ISFP; Ni is fourth for ESTP and third for ISFP. Both shared processes sit in different places, and the distribution of the first two and last two is not a simple reversal.

The judging functions are two different combinations: Ti and Fe for ESTP, Fi and Te for ISFP. Describing this as "Ti and Fi swapping, Fe and Te swapping" suggests one set of functions changing seats, but the positions also differ. ESTP has Ti second and Fe third. ISFP has Fi first and Te fourth.

That clears up a common confusion: both are said to "live in the moment", but Se carries a different weight. In this model, ESTP leads with Se and uses Ti as its auxiliary judging process. ISFP leads with Fi and uses Se as its auxiliary perceiving process. Either person can inspect a product and weigh whether it suits their needs. That is emphasis inside the model, not "what happens first".

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables. This page uses the common version, and a table that gives only the function name without an attitude should not surprise anyone; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early anyone speaks. Function positions do not predict a field of expertise, whether a collaboration runs smoothly, or who attracts whom. Base descriptions are in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
When the two work together, what goes well and what sticks both come down to the same material being read with two different emphases, not to ability. Both scenes below are fictional, written to illustrate possible trade-offs.

### Shooting a 15-second clip for a new product

(Fictional scene.) The same hand wash, the same phone, the same two days, the same launch date. One approach puts effort into comparable effects: shoot three different openings — a pump of gel, water rinsing, a close-up of the bottle — test them at small scale on the same account, see which opening holds more of the target audience, then decide which one to extend. The other puts effort into a unified feeling: decide first what this clip should make people feel — the freshness after rinsing, or the shock of cold water in winter — then choose the light, the background, and whether to keep only water sound or add music.

The first is efficient, at the cost of three pieces with inconsistent style that look like three brands when cut together; the second has presence as a finished film, at the cost of a reshoot rather than a re-edit if the feeling is wrong. Neither cost is about type; both depend on the deadline and the room to reshoot.

The verification aligns metrics with the plan, not with anyone's type. The two clips answer two questions: can the opening hold the target audience, and can viewers feel the intended freshness. If viewers need to recognise the product, ask what kind of product they saw. If the goal is brand recognition, ask which brand they remember. Keep those measures separate from the intended mood. A small-scale test only means something when enough feedback comes back; with too little, ask the same group of target viewers to watch both versions and answer the same questions.

The division follows the needs of the project, experience and willingness, not type: whoever knows distribution better, whoever understands this product's tone better, whoever has time these two days, owns that stretch; both share one acceptance standard, and both sets of metrics have to pass. Before shooting, each writes one sentence describing what failure would look like; if one lands on "nobody watched to the end" and the other on "this is not what we are", the two need different metrics filled in, not a verdict on who is right.

### Whether to book the anniversary ahead

(Fictional scene.) Three years together, and the anniversary falls on a Wednesday. Either may book ahead and either may leave it to the day — P describes keeping options outward, not an inability to plan, so the timing of a booking cannot separate these two types. What needs discussing is something else: how to weigh the risk of losing a table against how the day should feel.

One weighing values room that day: leave work early, find somewhere nearby with space, stay longer if the atmosphere is good, move on if not. The cost is that the popular places are full and they may end up picking up dinner at a convenience store. The other weighing values whether the place is right: scroll through reviews and photographs for a long time to be sure the other will like it. The cost is discovering the day before that everything is booked, and both feel awkward.

A workable move writes two dates separately: the latest date for locking in a fallback, by which a table is booked whether or not the ideal one was found; and the restaurant's own free-cancellation deadline, before which it can still be changed. Check both dates separately. A booking may have a different cancellation deadline from the date you set for choosing a fallback. The arrangement can be tried for a while — a floor for the spontaneous one and a deadline for the particular one; if it does not wear well, change it rather than treating it as a rule.

As for "why did you not reply to my message", that friction may appear and may have nothing to do with the booking — it is more often about who was busy and who was waiting for an answer, and should not be generalised into a fixed pattern of how these two types get along.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is taking E and I as "sociable" and "glum". E/I describes whether attention and energy go more to outward interaction or back to inner reflection; ISFP can be the most uninhibited person at a music festival, and ESTP can sit alone by the sea for an afternoon without a word. Type dynamics also speaks of a dominant process facing outward or inward, but that is a function-model statement and cannot be lifted directly into a definition of the letter preference.

The second misread is taking T and F as "rational" and "emotional". T/F describes whether judgement weighs a consistently applicable standard or people and values; both types can state a reason clearly, and both lose the thread when tired. Do not infer "reads the mood fast" from third-position Fe, or "does not count the cost" from fourth-position Te — expression, noticing and calculation are ability and experience, not preference.

The third slip is labelling by taste or hobby. Dressing well and taking good photographs are not reserved for ISFP, and sport and risk are not the patent of ESTP. What someone enjoys does not show what they decide by.

The fourth is treating "fast to react, dislikes planning" as evidence of the shared S and P. S is sourcing and P is outward stance; either may plan a trip in advance, and either may take over quickly in an emergency. Judging by speed or by planning gets both wrong.

body: When the two work together, what goes well and what sticks both come down to the same material being read with two different emphases, not to ability. Both scenes below are fictional, written to illustrate possible trade-offs.
### Shooting a 15-second clip for a new product

(Fictional scene.) The same hand wash, the same phone, the same two days, the same launch date. One approach puts effort into comparable effects: shoot three different openings — a pump of gel, water rinsing, a close-up of the bottle — test them at small scale on the same account, see which opening holds more of the target audience, then decide which one to extend. The other puts effort into a unified feeling: decide first what this clip should make people feel — the freshness after rinsing, or the shock of cold water in winter — then choose the light, the background, and whether to keep only water sound or add music.

The first is efficient, at the cost of three pieces with inconsistent style that look like three brands when cut together; the second has presence as a finished film, at the cost of a reshoot rather than a re-edit if the feeling is wrong. Neither cost is about type; both depend on the deadline and the room to reshoot.

The verification aligns metrics with the plan, not with anyone's type. The two clips answer two questions: can the opening hold the target audience, and can viewers feel the intended freshness. If viewers need to recognise the product, ask what kind of product they saw. If the goal is brand recognition, ask which brand they remember. Keep those measures separate from the intended mood. A small-scale test only means something when enough feedback comes back; with too little, ask the same group of target viewers to watch both versions and answer the same questions.

The division follows the needs of the project, experience and willingness, not type: whoever knows distribution better, whoever understands this product's tone better, whoever has time these two days, owns that stretch; both share one acceptance standard, and both sets of metrics have to pass. Before shooting, each writes one sentence describing what failure would look like; if one lands on "nobody watched to the end" and the other on "this is not what we are", the two need different metrics filled in, not a verdict on who is right.
### Whether to book the anniversary ahead

(Fictional scene.) Three years together, and the anniversary falls on a Wednesday. Either may book ahead and either may leave it to the day — P describes keeping options outward, not an inability to plan, so the timing of a booking cannot separate these two types. What needs discussing is something else: how to weigh the risk of losing a table against how the day should feel.

One weighing values room that day: leave work early, find somewhere nearby with space, stay longer if the atmosphere is good, move on if not. The cost is that the popular places are full and they may end up picking up dinner at a convenience store. The other weighing values whether the place is right: scroll through reviews and photographs for a long time to be sure the other will like it. The cost is discovering the day before that everything is booked, and both feel awkward.

A workable move writes two dates separately: the latest date for locking in a fallback, by which a table is booked whether or not the ideal one was found; and the restaurant's own free-cancellation deadline, before which it can still be changed. Check both dates separately. A booking may have a different cancellation deadline from the date you set for choosing a fallback. The arrangement can be tried for a while — a floor for the spontaneous one and a deadline for the particular one; if it does not wear well, change it rather than treating it as a rule.

body: Either person may enjoy a last-minute outing or prefer to make plans. What friends notice in one setting does not establish an E/I or T/F preference.

The resemblance comes from the shared S and P. S is sourcing: both more often trust comparable facts and first-hand experience, and neither is much moved by abstract argument. P is outward stance: both more often leave the conclusion until there is enough information, and neither rushes to nail down a schedule or a plan. But those two describe sourcing and stance only, not reaction speed, and not who is more fun — either can plan ahead, and either can act at once when needed.

The difference sits on two axes. E/I is the direction of attention and energy: outward to interaction and the situation, or inward to reflection and one's own experience. T/F is the basis for judgement: whether one standard can be applied consistently, or what this means for the people involved and for what one values. Both axes are used at once; the difference is which is relied on more often.
### One budget, and how to explain "meets spec but not right"

Suppose each is buying a common household appliance, with the same budget, the same use, and the same product pages and reviews. The difference is not who starts looking first, but how each explains "the specs all pass, and it still does not feel right".

One explanation starts more often from checkable conditions: which scenarios this specification covers, whether the missing feature will stick in some use, what the extra money buys, and whether the return policy is clear. The other starts more often from one's own experience and what one cares about: how the last one felt to use, whether this one will get in the way of daily life, and which details one genuinely does not want to compromise on.

Each has a cost. Watching only conditions may bring home something that passes everywhere and is never wanted; going only by fit may mean comparing for a long time and then not buying at all — "I have not met the right one" — or paying more than necessary for one moment of delight. Conversely, either person might focus on value for money when rent is due or compare several models carefully when the choice matters to them. Those are ability and circumstance, not evidence of preference.

What matters is not who is more particular, but which basis is cited first in this trade-off, and where each would give way: accepting a little dislike once the conditions pass, or accepting a little imperfection once it feels right. Both concessions occur in the same person.
### Why Se and Ni are shared while the whole judging set changes

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te. Position by position: Se is dominant for ESTP and second for ISFP; Ni is fourth for ESTP and third for ISFP. Both shared processes sit in different places, and the distribution of the first two and last two is not a simple reversal.

The judging functions are two different combinations: Ti and Fe for ESTP, Fi and Te for ISFP. Describing this as "Ti and Fi swapping, Fe and Te swapping" suggests one set of functions changing seats, but the positions also differ. ESTP has Ti second and Fe third. ISFP has Fi first and Te fourth.

That clears up a common confusion: both are said to "live in the moment", but Se carries a different weight. In this model, ESTP leads with Se and uses Ti as its auxiliary judging process. ISFP leads with Fi and uses Se as its auxiliary perceiving process. Either person can inspect a product and weigh whether it suits their needs. That is emphasis inside the model, not "what happens first".

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables. This page uses the common version, and a table that gives only the function name without an attitude should not surprise anyone; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early anyone speaks. Function positions do not predict a field of expertise, whether a collaboration runs smoothly, or who attracts whom. Base descriptions are in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp).

body: When the two work together, what goes well and what sticks both come down to the same material being read with two different emphases, not to ability. Both scenes below are fictional, written to illustrate possible trade-offs.
### Shooting a 15-second clip for a new product

(Fictional scene.) The same hand wash, the same phone, the same two days, the same launch date. One approach puts effort into comparable effects: shoot three different openings — a pump of gel, water rinsing, a close-up of the bottle — test them at small scale on the same account, see which opening holds more of the target audience, then decide which one to extend. The other puts effort into a unified feeling: decide first what this clip should make people feel — the freshness after rinsing, or the shock of cold water in winter — then choose the light, the background, and whether to keep only water sound or add music.

The first is efficient, at the cost of three pieces with inconsistent style that look like three brands when cut together; the second has presence as a finished film, at the cost of a reshoot rather than a re-edit if the feeling is wrong. Neither cost is about type; both depend on the deadline and the room to reshoot.

The verification aligns metrics with the plan, not with anyone's type. The two clips answer two questions: can the opening hold the target audience, and can viewers feel the intended freshness. If viewers need to recognise the product, ask what kind of product they saw. If the goal is brand recognition, ask which brand they remember. Keep those measures separate from the intended mood. A small-scale test only means something when enough feedback comes back; with too little, ask the same group of target viewers to watch both versions and answer the same questions.

The division follows the needs of the project, experience and willingness, not type: whoever knows distribution better, whoever understands this product's tone better, whoever has time these two days, owns that stretch; both share one acceptance standard, and both sets of metrics have to pass. Before shooting, each writes one sentence describing what failure would look like; if one lands on "nobody watched to the end" and the other on "this is not what we are", the two need different metrics filled in, not a verdict on who is right.
### Whether to book the anniversary ahead

(Fictional scene.) Three years together, and the anniversary falls on a Wednesday. Either may book ahead and either may leave it to the day — P describes keeping options outward, not an inability to plan, so the timing of a booking cannot separate these two types. What needs discussing is something else: how to weigh the risk of losing a table against how the day should feel.

One weighing values room that day: leave work early, find somewhere nearby with space, stay longer if the atmosphere is good, move on if not. The cost is that the popular places are full and they may end up picking up dinner at a convenience store. The other weighing values whether the place is right: scroll through reviews and photographs for a long time to be sure the other will like it. The cost is discovering the day before that everything is booked, and both feel awkward.

A workable move writes two dates separately: the latest date for locking in a fallback, by which a table is booked whether or not the ideal one was found; and the restaurant's own free-cancellation deadline, before which it can still be changed. Check both dates separately. A booking may have a different cancellation deadline from the date you set for choosing a fallback. The arrangement can be tried for a while — a floor for the spontaneous one and a deadline for the particular one; if it does not wear well, change it rather than treating it as a rule.

As for "why did you not reply to my message", that friction may appear and may have nothing to do with the booking — it is more often about who was busy and who was waiting for an answer, and should not be generalised into a fixed pattern of how these two types get along.

body: The first misread is taking E and I as "sociable" and "glum". E/I describes whether attention and energy go more to outward interaction or back to inner reflection; ISFP can be the most uninhibited person at a music festival, and ESTP can sit alone by the sea for an afternoon without a word. Type dynamics also speaks of a dominant process facing outward or inward, but that is a function-model statement and cannot be lifted directly into a definition of the letter preference.

The second misread is taking T and F as "rational" and "emotional". T/F describes whether judgement weighs a consistently applicable standard or people and values; both types can state a reason clearly, and both lose the thread when tired. Do not infer "reads the mood fast" from third-position Fe, or "does not count the cost" from fourth-position Te — expression, noticing and calculation are ability and experience, not preference.

The third slip is labelling by taste or hobby. Dressing well and taking good photographs are not reserved for ISFP, and sport and risk are not the patent of ESTP. What someone enjoys does not show what they decide by.

The fourth is treating "fast to react, dislikes planning" as evidence of the shared S and P. S is sourcing and P is outward stance; either may plan a trip in advance, and either may take over quickly in an emergency. Judging by speed or by planning gets both wrong.

The difference sits on two axes. E/I is the direction of attention and energy: outward to interaction and the situation, or inward to reflection and one's own experience. T/F is the basis for judgement: whether one standard can be applied consistently, or what this means for the people involved and for what one values. Both axes are used at once; the difference is which is relied on more often.

### One budget, and how to explain "meets spec but not right"

Suppose each is buying a common household appliance, with the same budget, the same use, and the same product pages and reviews. The difference is not who starts looking first, but how each explains "the specs all pass, and it still does not feel right".

One explanation starts more often from checkable conditions: which scenarios this specification covers, whether the missing feature will stick in some use, what the extra money buys, and whether the return policy is clear. The other starts more often from one's own experience and what one cares about: how the last one felt to use, whether this one will get in the way of daily life, and which details one genuinely does not want to compromise on.

Each has a cost. Watching only conditions may bring home something that passes everywhere and is never wanted; going only by fit may mean comparing for a long time and then not buying at all — "I have not met the right one" — or paying more than necessary for one moment of delight. Conversely, either person might focus on value for money when rent is due or compare several models carefully when the choice matters to them. Those are ability and circumstance, not evidence of preference.

What matters is not who is more particular, but which basis is cited first in this trade-off, and where each would give way: accepting a little dislike once the conditions pass, or accepting a little imperfection once it feels right. Both concessions occur in the same person.

### Why Se and Ni are shared while the whole judging set changes

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te. Position by position: Se is dominant for ESTP and second for ISFP; Ni is fourth for ESTP and third for ISFP. Both shared processes sit in different places, and the distribution of the first two and last two is not a simple reversal.

The judging functions are two different combinations: Ti and Fe for ESTP, Fi and Te for ISFP. Describing this as "Ti and Fi swapping, Fe and Te swapping" suggests one set of functions changing seats, but the positions also differ. ESTP has Ti second and Fe third. ISFP has Fi first and Te fourth.

That clears up a common confusion: both are said to "live in the moment", but Se carries a different weight. In this model, ESTP leads with Se and uses Ti as its auxiliary judging process. ISFP leads with Fi and uses Se as its auxiliary perceiving process. Either person can inspect a product and weigh whether it suits their needs. That is emphasis inside the model, not "what happens first".

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables. This page uses the common version, and a table that gives only the function name without an attitude should not surprise anyone; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early anyone speaks. Function positions do not predict a field of expertise, whether a collaboration runs smoothly, or who attracts whom. Base descriptions are in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp).

Align the conditions first: the same item, the same budget, the same product pages and reviews, the same return window. If one already knows this category well, or the other person is paying this time, role and experience will cover both columns.

Each row is a shared decision point, the two columns are the bases each may attend to, and the last column names the axis. Both types can use the other column; the table records only which is taken first more often.

| Shared decision point (one item, one budget, the same information) | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | ISFP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether to replace it now | May clarify how the same replacement options would work by talking them through | May clarify how the same options would work by reflecting privately | E/I: making sense of the same options through interaction or reflection |
| Several models all pass — which one | Which specification decides whether the most common use is covered | Which one is closer to what has felt right in use | S: shared sourcing; this row does not discriminate |
| The seller says "the specification is met" | Under what conditions that specification holds, and whether it applies consistently | Whether that specification actually suits this household | T/F: a checkable standard, or fit with people and values |
| The price runs a little over budget | Whether the same rule for approving an overrun would justify paying extra for either model | Whether the extra cost is worthwhile for what matters most to the household | T/F: different bases; both set a budget ceiling |
| Someone recommends another model | May clarify how the recommendation applies by discussing the same examples with the person who made it | May clarify how the recommendation applies by reflecting on those same examples | E/I: processing the same recommendation. Anyone can ask for concrete examples. |
| Thinking back a week later | Whether its observed performance meets the same criteria agreed before purchase | Whether using it every day supports priorities such as convenience or comfort | T/F: compare agreed performance criteria and what matters to the people using it |

sections.body_md:
When the two work together, what goes well and what sticks both come down to the same material being read with two different emphases, not to ability. Both scenes below are fictional, written to illustrate possible trade-offs.

### Shooting a 15-second clip for a new product

(Fictional scene.) The same hand wash, the same phone, the same two days, the same launch date. One approach puts effort into comparable effects: shoot three different openings — a pump of gel, water rinsing, a close-up of the bottle — test them at small scale on the same account, see which opening holds more of the target audience, then decide which one to extend. The other puts effort into a unified feeling: decide first what this clip should make people feel — the freshness after rinsing, or the shock of cold water in winter — then choose the light, the background, and whether to keep only water sound or add music.

The first is efficient, at the cost of three pieces with inconsistent style that look like three brands when cut together; the second has presence as a finished film, at the cost of a reshoot rather than a re-edit if the feeling is wrong. Neither cost is about type; both depend on the deadline and the room to reshoot.

The verification aligns metrics with the plan, not with anyone's type. The two clips answer two questions: can the opening hold the target audience, and can viewers feel the intended freshness. If viewers need to recognise the product, ask what kind of product they saw. If the goal is brand recognition, ask which brand they remember. Keep those measures separate from the intended mood. A small-scale test only means something when enough feedback comes back; with too little, ask the same group of target viewers to watch both versions and answer the same questions.

The division follows the needs of the project, experience and willingness, not type: whoever knows distribution better, whoever understands this product's tone better, whoever has time these two days, owns that stretch; both share one acceptance standard, and both sets of metrics have to pass. Before shooting, each writes one sentence describing what failure would look like; if one lands on "nobody watched to the end" and the other on "this is not what we are", the two need different metrics filled in, not a verdict on who is right.

### Whether to book the anniversary ahead

(Fictional scene.) Three years together, and the anniversary falls on a Wednesday. Either may book ahead and either may leave it to the day — P describes keeping options outward, not an inability to plan, so the timing of a booking cannot separate these two types. What needs discussing is something else: how to weigh the risk of losing a table against how the day should feel.

One weighing values room that day: leave work early, find somewhere nearby with space, stay longer if the atmosphere is good, move on if not. The cost is that the popular places are full and they may end up picking up dinner at a convenience store. The other weighing values whether the place is right: scroll through reviews and photographs for a long time to be sure the other will like it. The cost is discovering the day before that everything is booked, and both feel awkward.

A workable move writes two dates separately: the latest date for locking in a fallback, by which a table is booked whether or not the ideal one was found; and the restaurant's own free-cancellation deadline, before which it can still be changed. Check both dates separately. A booking may have a different cancellation deadline from the date you set for choosing a fallback. The arrangement can be tried for a while — a floor for the spontaneous one and a deadline for the particular one; if it does not wear well, change it rather than treating it as a rule.

As for "why did you not reply to my message", that friction may appear and may have nothing to do with the booking — it is more often about who was busy and who was waiting for an answer, and should not be generalised into a fixed pattern of how these two types get along.

sections.body_md:
The first misread is taking E and I as "sociable" and "glum". E/I describes whether attention and energy go more to outward interaction or back to inner reflection; ISFP can be the most uninhibited person at a music festival, and ESTP can sit alone by the sea for an afternoon without a word. Type dynamics also speaks of a dominant process facing outward or inward, but that is a function-model statement and cannot be lifted directly into a definition of the letter preference.

The second misread is taking T and F as "rational" and "emotional". T/F describes whether judgement weighs a consistently applicable standard or people and values; both types can state a reason clearly, and both lose the thread when tired. Do not infer "reads the mood fast" from third-position Fe, or "does not count the cost" from fourth-position Te — expression, noticing and calculation are ability and experience, not preference.

The third slip is labelling by taste or hobby. Dressing well and taking good photographs are not reserved for ISFP, and sport and risk are not the patent of ESTP. What someone enjoys does not show what they decide by.

The fourth is treating "fast to react, dislikes planning" as evidence of the shared S and P. S is sourcing and P is outward stance; either may plan a trip in advance, and either may take over quickly in an emergency. Judging by speed or by planning gets both wrong.

When two results differ, confirm whether both used the same questionnaire, version and language, then which kind of situation you referred to: a project at work, or something at home. Item format and recent circumstances affect answers, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency; nor should the direction of the answer be inferred from occupation or social life.

If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at whether E/I and T/F sit near that tool's boundary; being near a boundary only means the item is sensitive to changes in your answers, not that two types both hold. If you retest, follow the interval and method in the tool's notes; this page gives no universal timetable.

Change the way you keep the record: take a few recent trade-offs — buying something, taking on a job, agreeing to a gathering — and write three lines for each: what information you trusted, what standard decided it, and what would change your mind. What is written is the basis and the conditions, not the sequence of actions. If "can this standard be applied consistently" or "what does this mean for the people involved" keeps recurring, that is worth discussing as your judging habit; it is not a typing rule and is not scored.

items.answer:
E/I and T/F; S and P are shared.

The confusion comes mostly from the shared S and P making the two alike in sourcing and outward stance: both look at the facts first, and neither rushes to close the discussion. What actually separates them is two things — whether attention and energy turn outward or inward, and whether judgement weighs a consistently applicable standard or people and values. Read those across comparable situations, not by reaction speed, and not by who states a reason first.
items.question: Which two letters differ, and why are they so easily confused?

items.answer:
Because Se sits in a different place for each, though a position describes emphasis in the model, not a scale of ability.

In the writing used here, Se is the dominant process for ESTP and the auxiliary for ISFP. Either person can use direct observations before making a choice. What makes the trade-offs look different is the judging basis: one more often asks whether the standard can be applied consistently, the other what this means for the people or things they value. Both can use the other basis; they simply take one first more often across many matters.
items.question: Both rely on Se — why do the trade-offs differ so much?

items.answer:
Yes, and both often appear in the same person.

That shows ability and preference are not the same thing: acting on a whim, comparing carefully, paying more for aesthetics and giving up a favourite for the budget are all done by both types. What discriminates better is the reason — across several comparable matters, did you drop something because the standard did not hold, or because it did not fit what you value. A single behaviour or one phrasing cannot type anyone.
items.question: ISFP also acts on a whim, and ESTP also chooses carefully?

items.answer:
Not by type, but by the needs of the project, experience and willingness.

Start by splitting acceptance into two parallel metrics: one asking whether the target audience stays past the opening, one asking whether the intended tone comes across; if recognition is also a goal, add a third. Both must pass, and who owns which stretch depends on who knows how and who has time. Both types can run a test, and both can hold a tone; the reverse is equally true.
items.question: For display work or shooting a clip, how do they divide it?

items.answer:
Both may book ahead and both may decide on the day — both are P, so the timing of a booking cannot carry the discrimination.

What this case really needs is how to weigh booking risk against the experience of the day: one values room to move, the other whether the place is right. A workable move writes "the latest date to lock a fallback" and "the restaurant's free-cancellation deadline" separately, booking a cancellable table by the date and changing it afterwards; that is an arrangement worth trying, not a rule guaranteed to work for both.
items.question: Living together, where does the rhythm differ?

If the tool reports dimension scores, look at whether E/I and T/F sit near its boundary; being near it only means the item is sensitive to changes in your answers, and cannot establish that both types hold. If you retest, follow the tool's notes; no unsupported universal interval is prescribed, and the direction of the answer should not be inferred from the nature of your work or how often you socialise.

The official material supports the preference definitions and the dynamics framework; it does not endorse typing anyone from the behaviour in the fictional scenes here.

Four-position convention: Se–Ti–Fe–Ni for ESTP and Fi–Se–Ni–Te for ISFP are the common writing adopted here, and the attitude of the third process in particular is handled differently across sources; this page does not present the arrangement as the Foundation's only version, nor use positions to infer behavioural order, a field of expertise, collaboration or attraction.

Editorial fiction: the short clip and the anniversary are editorial fictions, corresponding to no real person, brand or project, written to illustrate possible trade-offs.

Scope limits: assessment results are not for ranking ability, screening candidates or predicting relationships; anything involving clinical judgement belongs to qualified professionals.
